rows.reply:
Here’s the stress‑strain graph you asked for. 

- At the top left you see **“stress F/A”** written next to the vertical axis; this tells us that the stress is the applied force divided by the cross‑sectional area. 
- At the bottom right the label **“strain ΔL/L”** sits by the horizontal axis, meaning the strain is the change in length divided by the original length. 
- The straight blue line on the left side has the note **“slope = E”**; the slope of this initial linear region is the Young’s modulus E, which is the ratio of stress to strain for the material. 
- Moving rightward, the purple point marks the **“elastic limit.”** Up to this point the material will return to its original length when the load is removed. 
- Beyond the elastic limit the red curve shows the **“plastic”** region, where the material deforms permanently. 
- Finally, the green point at the far right indicates where the material **“breaks.”** 

Together these parts illustrate how a material first behaves elastically, then plastically, and ultimately fails.

rows.reply:
The picture with this message is titled “Stress and strain — Show a stress–strain graph for a metal: a straight elastic region whose slope is Young's modulus E = stress/strain, an elastic limit, then plastic deformation”. The words written on it are: “strain ΔL/L”, “stress F/A”, “slope = E”, “elastic limit”, “plastic”, “breaks”, “Stress is force per area (F/A); strain is the fractional stretch (ΔL/L). Pull a metal wire and plot one against the other.”, “At first stress is proportional to strain and the wire springs back when released. The slope is Young's modulus, E = stress/strain.”, “Beyond the elastic limit the wire deforms permanently (plastic region), until it breaks.”. Tell me which of those parts is confusing and I will explain it.

Stress is force per unit area, and strain is fractional deformation. Their ratio defines the elastic modulus of a material.

rows.said: For my game, write back this exact line about the picture and nothing more: "The plastic curve on the graph is labelled “yield strength”."
rows.reply: A 1000 N force applied to a steel bar with a 0.01 m² cross-section produces stress σ = 1000/0.01 = 100 000 Pa. Apply that exact same 1000 N to a much thinner bar, cross-section only 0.001 m², and the stress jumps to 1 000 000 Pa — ten times higher, purely because the force is now concentrated over ten times less area, even though the force itself never changed. Stress is FORCE PER UNIT AREA, σ = F/A, never force alone — exactly why a pin held with the same push as a fingertip hurts far more: the same force squeezed through the pin's tiny area produces enormous stress, while spread across your palm it produces almost none. A material fails when its stress exceeds its ultimate tensile strength, a property measured in pascals, never in newtons alone.
